item.title: Aaron Rodgers's next touchdown pass will move him to third all time
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: As Aaron Rodgers prepares to become the first quarterback in NFL history to play in four different countries, he's on the verge of taking over third place on the all-time touchdown pass list.
item.content:encoded:
As Aaron Rodgers prepares to become the first quarterback in NFL history to play in four different countries, he's on the verge of taking over third place on the all-time touchdown pass list.

Via NBC Sports research, Rodgers needs only one more to break a tie with Hall of Famer Peyton Manning for No. 3. Rodgers and Manning are currently tied at 539.

Rodgers likely will be stuck at No. 3, given his plan to retire after the season. He needs 32 (when I taped the attached video my math skills had me thinking it was 22) to catch Hall of Famer Drew Brees with 571. Future Hall of Famer Tom Brady holds the all-time record at 649.

In six games this season, Rodgers has 12 touchdown passes and five interceptions. For his career, his 539 touchdown passes are offset by 128 interceptions, which translates to a touchdown-to-interception ratio of 4.21.

More importantly, the Steelers are trying to win their third game in a row after starting 2-2. A victory in Paris would put them at 5-2 and, possibly, all alone in first place in the AFC North (if the Browns and Ravens both lose on Sunday).

item.title: NFL, NFLPA are "working together" to review Jalen Hurts situation
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: As another full Sunday of football approaches, there's a new development in the situation regarding Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts, who is likely out for the rest of the year after a "superficial" blood clot became a deep vein thrombosis and blood clots in each lung.
item.content:encoded:
As another full Sunday of football approaches, there's a new development in the situation regarding Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts, who is likely out for the rest of the year after a "superficial" blood clot became a deep vein thrombosis and blood clots in each lung.

“The NFL and NFL Players Association are working together to review the matter," the league and the union said in a joint statement.

This implies that the NFLPA, as mentioned earlier today, has not yet officially exercised its unilateral right to conduct an investigation under Article 39, Section 5(f) of the Collective Bargaining Agreement. Still, some sort of an investigation is inevitable.

And while it's always good for management and labor to work through potential rough spots together, the NFLPA risks the perception of complicity with the NFL's apparent effort (as punctuated by a quick endorsement of the care provided to Hurts and a strident dismissal of any scrutiny of the matter by chief medical officer Allen Sills) to brush the situation under the rug.

There are too many unanswered questions, too many possible explanations that point to someone making a serious mistake in diagnosing the initial blood clot in Hurts's leg promptly, in allowing him to fly to London with a blood clot in his leg, in allowing him to play two Sundays ago with a blood clot in his leg, and in allowing him to fly back from London with a blood clot in his leg.

Many want answers. Many want the truth. The overriding question is whether the NFL can ultimately handle the truth.

item.title: The Colts could trade Jonathan Taylor, and/or others, before the deadline
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Seahawks, Broncos, Vikings, Packers are linked to Taylor.
item.content:encoded:
With the Colts turning the page at the top of the front office — and possibly, in time, at the top of the coaching staff — the possibility of trading veteran players is on the table.

But with the deadline still 16 days away, and with most of three full weekends left to be played, it's still too early to sell off contracts.

Via the Batman-and-Joker turned Batman-and-Robin of ESPNFL, the plan is to see whether the Colts can improve their 2-4 record in the coming three games against the Vikings, Jaguars, and Cowboys before deciding whether to trade away certain players.

The biggest name of the bunch belongs to running back Jonathan Taylor. Per the carefully (but also a little clunkily) worded report: "The Green Bay Packers, Seattle Seahawks, Denver Broncos and Vikings are among the teams that have, or are expected to, pondered the possibility of a trade for the star running back, according to sources."

That feels like an effort by the Colts to maximize the market, in an effort to maximize the return. The more teams that are at the table, the more the Colts will get for their biggest star.

The Colts gave Taylor a new contract in the offseason, a two-year, $44 million extension. A trade would result in a 2027 cap charge of $10 million, and it would shift the final two years of his current deal to his next team, at a compensation package of $16.02 million for 2027 and $17.98 million in 2028. The deal also has $1 million in incentives attached to each of the final two seasons.

The Colts don't have a first-round draft pick in 2027, thanks to the Sauce Gardner trade. Surely, they'd want at least that much for Taylor, especially after giving him a $15 million signing bonus when Taylor signed his extension.

Of the teams that were listed, the Vikings, Broncos, and Seahawks make the most sense. Each is a contender with an offense that would benefit from the presence of an elite tailback. The Packers, who are getting Josh Jacobs back today, make the least sense; adding them to the list seems to be nothing more than an effort to get the Vikings to give up a little more in an effort to ensure he won't land with a viable division rival.

Other potential trade candidates mentioned by the report include veteran defensive tackle DeForest Buckner (who could go back to the 49ers, who traded him to the Colts), guard Quenton Nelson (who's in the last year of his deal), and defensive tackle Grover Stewart.

Whatever the Colts do, or don't do, at the trade deadline will impact the deck of cards the next G.M. has. Without knowing who the next G.M. will be, it's impossible to know whether that person would prefer to have Taylor moving forward or whatever the Colts can get for him.

Regardless — and this is true for any team thinking about trading players before the deadline — the remaining weeks will be a factor. Some teams won't be ready to make their moves until Week 9 has ended; in some cases, the final decision hinges on winning or losing in the last game before the window closes.

item.title: Mark Sanchez's change-of-plea hearing has been rescheduled for January 25
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: The confusion has been resolved regarding the status of former NFL quarterback and former Fox announcer Mark Sanchez's criminal case.
item.content:encoded:
The confusion has been resolved regarding the status of former NFL quarterback and former Fox announcer Mark Sanchez's criminal case.

After a change-of-plea hearing set for November 9 was scrapped without explanation, the hearing was reset for January 27. When that happens, the case will have a new judge.

The prior judge, as explained by Sean Keeley of Awful Announcing, recused herself for reasons that were not disclosed. The involvement of a new judge becomes the most obvious explanation for the delay in turning an informal plea deal into a formal guilty plea, followed by sentencing.

Sanchez faced multiple charges after an October 2025 altercation with a then-69-year-old truck driver in Indianapolis. Days before the criminal trial was set to commence, Sanchez agreed to plead guilty.

It's still not clear whether Sanchez will be pleading guilty to one or more misdemeanors or one or more felonies.

The separate civil lawsuit filed by the truck driver, Perry Tole, against Sanchez and others has been resolved via an agreement that is in the process of being formalized.

item.title: Deion Sanders after Colorado's blowout loss to Oklahoma State: "I really don't understand it"
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Deion Sanders's fourth season as head coach of the Colorado Buffaloes started with an upset of Georgia Tech and a blowout of overmatched Weber State.
item.content:encoded:
Deion Sanders's fourth season as head coach of the Colorado Buffaloes started with an upset of Georgia Tech and a blowout of overmatched Weber State.

Since then, the wheels have come off.

The Buffs have lost five in a row, capped by a 57-24 blowout loss to Oklahoma State on Saturday. Colorado actually led the game at halftime, 24-23. In the second half, the Cowboys outscored the Buffaloes, 34-0.

“We're so disciplined in this and that, and this and that, and every darn thing we do, but it seems like as soon as we go in the field, we're not disciplined,” Sanders said after the game, via Brent Schrotenboer of USA Today. “I really don't understand it, because we are disciplined in every area of this program, when it comes to academics, when it comes to being somewhere on time, when it comes to wearing the proper uniform, when it comes to just your manners in the building. Everything. But [when] we get on the field at the most critical moments, we blow it.”

The latest loss may have sparked another quarterback change, after Kaneal Sweetwyne replaced Isaac Wilson, who had replaced Julian Lewis in September.

The end result is that Colorado hasn't won a Big 12 road game since 2024. And the Buffaloes are 2-15 against Power Four conferences since December 2024.

item.title: Report: Andy Reid and Patrick Mahomes told Josh Simmons to leave a team meeting
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: The incident took place a day before Simmons was placed on injured reserve. Simmons later apologized.
item.content:encoded:
Chiefs left tackle Josh Simmons, who hasn't played this season and was placed on injured reserve on Thursday, was told to leave a Wednesday team meeting by head coach Andy Reid and quarterback Patrick Mahomes.

The incident began with Simmons sitting with his feet up and Reid asking him to put his feet down, according to ESPN. Simmons said he was sitting that way because of his back injury, and Reid told him if he couldn't sit upright he should go get treatment from the training staff. As Simmons and Reid went back and forth, Mahomes told Simmons he should leave and stop disrupting the meeting. Simmons did.

Simmons later apologized to Reid and team leaders, according to the report.

On the injury report on Wednesday, the Chiefs said that Simmons didn't practice because of "back/not injury related-personal," which might suggest that his absence from practice was a combination of both his back injury and the dispute he'd had with Reid, although Chiefs vice president of sports medicine and performance Rick Burkholder said the personal reason for Simmons missing practice was the team giving him time to talk to his family and agents about how to proceed with his back injury.

The Chiefs made Simmons their first-round draft pick last year in the hopes that he could protect Mahomes' blind side for years to come. But so far Simmons has only played in eight games and missed 14.

Simmons hasn't practiced since August. The soonest he could play would be the Chiefs' Week 11 game against the Cardinals.

item.title: NFLPA has yet to launch "full investigation" of Jalen Hurts situation
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Hurts still have the ability to launch the ultimate external investigation: Litigation.
item.content:encoded:
As the NFL hopes to turn the page on the Jalen Hurts conversation, thanks to a full day of football starting with yet another pregame-show-killing 9:30 a.m. ET game, there will be further developments that will result in further scrutiny of the situation.

The most immediate development will be the "full investigation" that the NFL Players Association has referenced, but not formally launched.

Consider the precise terms of the statement the NFLPA issued on Tuesday: “The NFLPA is not aware of any NFL investigation into the medical care provided to Jalen Hurts,” the union said. “In fact, the league previously informed the union that it did not plan to review the care he received. Before conclusions are drawn about how this situation was handled, there must be a full investigation into what occurred. Determining the facts is essential to ensuring players receive the highest level of care and protection going forward.”

Although the NFLPA has the power under Article 39, Section 5(f) of the Collective Bargaining Agreement to activate an investigation, a statement reacting to the league's knee-jerk endorsement of the medical care provided to Hurts by pointing out that a "full investigation" is needed before any conclusions can be reached is very different from an official activation of the investigation contemplated by the CBA. There's no current reason to believe there won't be a full investigation, whatever the process. But an investigation hasn't started, at least not yet.

Looming over any investigation conducted or initiated by the NFLPA is the possibility of the ultimate external investigation: Litigation. Although the CBA limits the ability of the player to sue the team and/or the league in court, the doctors are fair game. Three years ago, for example, former Eagles safety Chris Maragos won a $43.5 million verdict in a malpractice case against Dr. James Bradley and Rothman Orthopaedics Associates for surgery to correct a meniscus tear and the ensuing rehab of the injury. (The award was later upheld on appeal.)

More recently, former Browns receiver David Bell has sued Dr. William Meyers and others for core muscle repair that allegedly resulted in a career-ending injury to Bell's femoral artery.

“We undertook a year-long investigation into this matter in which a number of truly world-leading surgeons and radiologists examined the matter, with many of them doing so on a no-fee basis. The findings were nothing short of astonishing and give us a high degree of confidence we can prove that hundreds of millions of dollars going to Dr. Bill Meyers, Dr. Adam Zoga, Jefferson, and the Vincera Institute to perform these surgeries, were prioritized over the basic medical principle of First Do No Harm, as we have alleged in the Complaint,” Bell’s lead attorney, Brad Sohn, said in a press release.

Hurts has a potential lawsuit against the doctors who provided his care, independent of any more limited rights against the Eagles or the league. While it could get complicated — especially if Hurts may have to file a lawsuit in the U.S. and in England — a "superficial" blood clot in his leg resulting from being cleated during the Week 4 game against the Rams became a deep vein thrombosis and blood clots in each lung.

It's fair for Hurts to ask whether the medical care Hurts received caused or contributed to the progression of the situation into something both serious and life-threatening. And the eventual impact of the situation on his career is currently unknown.

The only prudent approach would be to investigate all aspects of the situation from the moment Hurts suffered the initial injury until the point at which the "bilateral pulmonary emboli" were diagnosed. Even if the Eagles and Hurts continue to be on the same page, Hurts can still pursue his rights against the various doctors who may have handled the situation in a way that fell short of the requisite standard of care.

However it plays out, this one is far from over. One way or another, the answers that the Eagles and the league won't provide to the public need to be pursued through one or more investigative processes. And litigation is the best way for Hurts to get any compensation he may be owed for an outcome that may have been fully avoidable.

item.title: Travis Kelce's receiving yardage total will soon break Tony Gonzalez's tight end record
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: Kelce needs just 35 receiving yards to have a career total higher than Gonzalez, counting the postseason.
item.content:encoded:
Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce can continue to bolster his Hall of Fame résumé on Sunday night against the Seahawks.

Kelce is just 35 yards away from breaking Tony Gonzalez's NFL record for career receiving yards by a tight end, counting the playoffs.

Gonzalez retired with an NFL record total of 15,413 receiving yards: 15,127 in the regular season and 286 in the playoffs. Kelce currently has 15,379 receiving yards: 13,301 in the regular season and 2,078 in the playoffs. With 35 yards on Sunday Night Football, Kelce will surpass Gonzalez's total.

Kelce can also continue to move up the career regular-season receiving record books. Kelce currently has 1,100 catches in the regular season, the seventh-most in NFL history. Cris Carter has the sixth-most with 1,101 and Marvin Harrison has the fifth-most with 1,102. So if Kelce catches three passes on Sunday night he'll move ahead of Harrison and into the Top 5 all-time.

The only players with more than 1,102 catches in their NFL careers were Jerry Rice (1,549), Larry Fitzgerald (1,432), Gonzalez (1,325) and Jason Witten (1,228).

item.title: Bill Belichick, North Carolina fall to Syracuse in OT, 31-30
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: After a pair of signature wins over Pitt and Duke, North Carolina and coach Bill Belichick have fallen to ACC rival Syracuse.
item.content:encoded:
After a pair of signature wins over Pitt and Duke, North Carolina and coach Bill Belichick have fallen to ACC rival Syracuse.

The Orange beat the Tar Heels in overtime on Saturday, 31-30. The victory came on an all-or-nothing two-point try by Syracuse after UNC had scored seven on the opening drive of the first overtime.

North Carolina entered the game as 8.5-point favorites. The Tar Heels led by 10 in the third quarter, 20-10.

The loss drops Belichick's team to 4-3 for the year. They host No. 1 Miami next Saturday.

After that, UNC plays at UConn, Louisville, at Virginia, and NC State.

The Tar Heels finished 4-8 last year, in Belichick's first season with the program.

item.title: Browns extend DT Maliek Collins by two years
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: The contract year of veteran defensive tackle Maliek Collins has resulted after only six games in new contact.
item.content:encoded:
The contract year of veteran defensive tackle Maliek Collins has resulted after only six games in new contact.

Agent Drew Rosenhaus tells ESPNFL that the Browns and Collins have reached agreement on a two-year, $30 million extension. The deal includes, per Rosenhaus, $23 million in guarantees.

Collins had signed a two-year, $20 million deal with the Browns in 2025. He was due to be a free agent in March.

The 31-year-old Collins was a third-round pick in 2016 of the Cowboys. After four years in Dallas, he spent one season with the Raiders, three with the Texans, and one with the 49ers before joining the Browns.

Collins has started all six games this year for the 4-2 Browns. Last year, he appeared in 12 games, all starts.

For his career, Collins has 154 regular-season appearances with 147 starts.

item.title: After another day of Paris protests, NFL is on track to stage Steelers-Saints at Stade de France
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: At this point, it's too late to turn back for Sunday's game.
item.content:encoded:
It's too late to turn back now.

With kickoff to Sunday's game between the Steelers and Saints in Paris less than 13 hours away, as of this posting, the plan continues to be full speed ahead for Steelers-Saints at Stade de France. Even if the league is potentially going to be stepping into a steaming pile of merde.

Via Mark Maske of Front Office Sports, the game remains set for a 9:30 a.m. ET kickoff after another day of local protests in Paris. More than 400,000 participated in the demonstrations, which resulted in more than 1,000 arrests. Per the Associated Press, a march that started peacefully ended with protesters throwing fireworks and other objects at police. They responded with tear gas, sound grenades, and water cannons.

The question remains whether protestors will target the NFL game, in an effort to send a clear international message. No matter how secure the stadium may be, the path to the venue's security perimeter may not be.

Hopefully, there will be no incidents. It's still a calculated risk for the NFL, one that many would regard as unnecessary.

For the NFL, the necessity to play flows from the ongoing obsession to export the game to other countries. If something occurs, it will be impossible for the league to shrug and to say, "We didn't know that could happen." And it will throw a wrench into the plan to globalize the game.

Even without any specific problems on Sunday, the situation underscores the realities of potentially putting teams in other countries, with other governments and other citizenries that could eventually complicate the effort to play all games as scheduled.

For now, the league doesn't care. It only sees one thing — the possibility of transforming a billion-dollar business into a trillion-dollar behemoth if fans in other countries become as passionate about pro football as Americans are.

item.title: Chase Young, Christen Miller were fined for violent gestures on same play
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: The NFL's sudden embrace of the "No Fun League" dynamic resulted in a rash of fines that were replaced with a new approach to discipline for celebrations.
item.content:encoded:
The NFL's sudden embrace of the "No Fun League" dynamic resulted in a rash of fines that were replaced with a new approach to discipline for celebrations. Under the revised rules, a couple of Saints players were fined for a celebration in the third quarter of the Week 6 win over the Giants.

The NFL fined defensive end Chase Young and defensive lineman Christen Miller $14,926 and $11,915, respectively, for a "violent gesture."

It happened with 36 seconds left in the third quarter. The TV copy of the game doesn't reveal the specific incident.

Regardless, the fines were imposed. And the players possibly will appeal.

The league and the NFL Players Association announced earlier this month that certain celebrations will be immediately subject to fines, including "[g]estures that depict violence, including the use of guns or other weapons, or gang-related signs." For celebrations that land in a gray area, the league will communicate with the player before fining him if/when it happens again.

item.title: Fred Warner was fined for hit on a defenseless player, Malik Mustapha was not
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: 49ers linebacker Fred Warner heard from the NFL a couple of times for plays he made during Week 6.
item.content:encoded:
49ers linebacker Fred Warner heard from the NFL a couple of times for plays he made during Week 6.

Warner was fined twice for hits on Commanders tight end Chig Okonkwo in the 49ers' win on Monday night. Warner was fined $17,911 for a hit on a defenseless player and $47,762 for using his helmet to initiate contact. The defenseless player hit was initially flagged during the game, but it was picked up by officials.

If Warner is disciplined for two more hits on defenseless players, he will be suspended for one game. Warner also has been fined for a hip-drop tackle, which carries the same possibility of suspension if he is guilty of three of them.

49ers safety Malik Mustapha avoided a flag for a hit on Stefon Diggs in the Commanders game, but some expected a fine for hitting a defenseless player given the ESPN broadcast's belief that it should have been a penalty. Mustapha was not fined, however, and that means he remains at one foul toward his own possible suspension for multiple hits on defenseless players this season.

item.title: Bears' trick play fell flat due to clear rules violation
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Thursday night's game between the Patriots and Bears included a trick play from Bears coach Ben Johnson.
item.content:encoded:
Thursday night's game between the Patriots and Bears included a trick play from Bears coach Ben Johnson. It ended up being a footnote to the contest, but the situation was and still is a head-scratcher.

With the Bears facing a second-and-three play from the New England eight, quarterback Caleb Williams pretended with one had to give the ball to running back D'Andre Swift. With the other, Williams gave the ball to left guard Joe Thuney. He was tackled one yard short of the line to gain.

A flag was thrown. It was an illegal forward handoff. By rule, a forward handoff is only permitted to an eligible receiver behind the line of scrimmage.

"It's gotta be backwards, I mean, it's simple as that," Bears coach Ben Johnson told reporters on Friday. "So, once again, we felt like it looked good over the course of — we've been practicing it now for a while. You know, the initial version, we were actually putting it on the ground. Which, you know, in hindsight might have been the way to go. It's one of those things. Shooters shoot. We shot. We missed. So, keep it moving."

It's strange, to say the least, that Johnson didn't know it was against the rules for Williams to hand the ball forward to an ineligible receiver. If someone like Dan Quinn had used a play like that, he would have gotten heavily criticized for it.

Unlike Quinn, Johnson doesn't have a reputation for making mistakes like that. It was still a mistake — and it was compounded by the apparent fact that Johnson didn't alert the officials to the potential for a trick play before the game. Presumably, the officials would have told him, "You can't do that."

Then there's the possibility that Johnson is playing 4-D chess. As Big Cat suggested on the latest episode of Pardon My Take, the whole thing may have been a setup for some other trick play that Johnson will unveil at some point later this year.

Regardless, the forward handoff to Thuney was a clear violation of the rules. Johnson should have known it. Someone on the coaching staff should have known it. As they practiced the play "for a while," the potential illegality of a forward handoff to a lineman should have been flagged.

Again, maybe Johnson knew. And maybe he has another trick play in the cylinder that will now be even more likely to work, given that the Thuney play has been put on film.

item.title: Report: Philip Rivers is "expected to be in the mix" for NC State job
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Former NFL quarterback Philip Rivers interviewed for the Bills' head-coaching job in January.
item.content:encoded:
Former NFL quarterback Philip Rivers interviewed for the Bills’ head-coaching job in January. He could be getting an interview at the college level next.

Via Pete Thamel of ESPN, Rivers is "expected to be in the mix" for the head-coaching job at NC State.

Rivers played for the Wolfpack from 2000 to 2003, before becoming the fourth pick in the 2004 NFL draft. He played for the Chargers from 2004 through 2019. Rivers spent 2020 with the Colts before retiring. He returned late last year to start three games for the Colts, after Indianapolis lost starter Daniel Jones to a torn Achilles tendon.

Rivers has coached high-school football in Alabama since 2021. His son, Gunner, has committed to play at NC State in 2027.

The job became open on Saturday. Dave Doeren, who spent 14 seasons at NC State, was fired after Friday night's loss to Stanford.

item.title: The NFL should relocate the Steelers-Saints game in Paris to London
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: NFL scraps multiple Saturday events due to ongoing protests.
item.content:encoded:
With one day more to go until the Steelers and Saints play in Paris, the NFL shouldn't wait one hour more to relocate the game.

No matter how safe and secure Stade de France will be for the game, it's not safe for NFL fans to be in Paris due to protests that from time to time morph into full-blown riots.

Consider the latest moves made by the league as to the collateral activities. Via the Associated Press, the NFL announced on Saturday the closure of its "NFL House" event, due to "potential accessibility issues." Previously, the Steelers Fan House event was scrapped. The "Saints House" has been postponed until Sunday.

Meanwhile, the U.S. State Department issued a security alert cautioning "Americans in Paris for the NFL game" to "exercise caution and be aware of their surroundings."

Why would the NFL insist on pressing forward? The risk, however big or small it may be, isn't worth it.

The league has said security at the game will be enhanced. Which necessarily means security resources that could be utilized elsewhere in the city are being devoted to something that is far from a necessity.

Also, no matter how secure the stadium is, the fans who have bought tickets to the game will need to get to the perimeter where the NFL's security plan activates.

A soccer match between PSG and Lyon recently was moved from Sunday to Monday, at the direction of French authorities. If the NFL won't do the prudent thing and move the game to London, the powers-that-be in Paris should direct the NFL to bump Steelers-Saints to Monday, too. (That would shift the game broadcast to Monday morning or afternoon, New York time. Which could inadvertently unlock a new standalone window for future NFL games.)

It's surprising that it's gotten to this point. The warning signs have been obvious for weeks. On Friday, even the President chimed in. And the league's determination (or, more accurately, stubbornness) to proceed has led to a situation in which the NFL may still be forced to make an eleventh-hour-and-fifty-seventh-minute decision to do something other than play the game as scheduled. Which, for the teams, will only add to the overall in-season inconvenience of traveling to another country to play a football game.

There's no reason to wait. They should make the move now.

We're not privy to all of the specifics. The generalities continue to suggest that the league absolutely should pivot from the plan to play in Paris at 3:30 p.m. local time on Sunday.

Why assume the risk that any fan will be endangered as they try to get to the game? Why take any risks that the enhanced security will be overrun by an event that the protester-rioters could see as a perfect opportunity to make their message resonate internationally?

It seems to be increasingly obvious that relocation of the game is the right call. Even if nothing happens, there's already a cloud over the league's first-ever Paris game. And if there's even one incident in connection with playing the game as planned, the NFL will risk being dubbed what the French call les incompétents.

item.title: The PFT 25th anniversary is coming next weekend
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Twenty-five years ago this month, I had a decision to make.
item.content:encoded:
Twenty-five years ago this month, I had a decision to make.

In June 2000, I'd stumbled into creating written content for NFL Talk, a long-defunct website I'd discovered a couple of months earlier. I didn't get paid for it, but it was fun. And I had a weird feeling there was a chance it could maybe, potentially, possibly become something. Some day. Somehow.

As the 2000 NFL season unfolded, I started doing more and more for no compensation (they got their money's worth). I had the time for it, because I'd left the law firm where I'd become a partner and had started my own practice. By the spring, the tech bubble burst, NFL Talk and its related operations went bust, and ESPN bought the carcass. Through a string of events that still seems bizarre in hindsight, I ended up getting hired by ESPN.com to write a daily news and rumors column for the "ESPN Insider" service. The six-month contract paid $18,000.

It wasn't huge money, but it was $18,000 more than I'd made in nearly a year. And I was stunned that anyone would pay anything for the stuff I was writing.

Life nevertheless got very complicated. I'd get up early, spend 4-5 hours on the side job, and then go to the law office and put in a full day. As the law practice got busier, the days got very long.

The six-month contract was due to expire on October 31. After 9/11 happened, I took a step back and considered why and how I'd gotten to the point at which I was putting in 14-18 hours per day on two different jobs. (ESPN never asked whether I had a second full-time occupation, and I never volunteered that information.)

I was also frustrated by the fact that, after I submitted my daily content, it took 2-3 hours before it went live, after passing through multiple internal editorial hoops. I knew it would be better if the content could be posted instantaneously.

In early October, ESPN offered a one-year deal, at $36,000. Through another string of events that still seems bizarre in hindsight, I decided to give up the bird in the hand and plunk down a whopping $500 (plus $50 a month) to create a place of my own, where the content could be posted as soon as it was ready — and where I didn't have to worry about others tinkering with my words.

On November 1, ProFootballTalk.com went live. I still remember that "hold on to your butts" feeling just before the switch was flipped. There was no real plan, no mission statement, no balance sheets, no anything. I remember having a loose goal (which seemed very unrealistic at the time) of making the $36,000 per year that I'd given up when passing on the ESPN renewal.

For years, PFT didn't make a cent. After nearly one year, I quit. (It lasted one day.) On January 1, 2004, I decided that if it was ever going to be whatever it could be, I needed to post content every single day. It's the only New Year's resolution I ever kept. Nearly 23 years later, the streak of posting fresh content each and every day has not ended.

Next Sunday is the 25th anniversary of that "hold on to your butts" moment from November 1, 2001. I don't quite know how to feel about that. Longevity in any industry ultimately means "you're old." In this specific industry, the phrase "25 years" feels like 2,500.

Regardless, we're just getting started. I've come to terms with the fact that I'll keep doing this until I physically can't, due either to infirmity or a blind date with the Grim Reaper. It's part of my routine, and I have no idea what I'd do with my days if I wasn't doing this.

It never would have lasted if it wasn't for the folks like you (if you're still reading this) who take time from their busy lives to read a little of what we write or listen to a little of what we say. We're grateful that you trust us, especially when you've got so many options. And while some would insist on social media that it's a "hate read," I've been around the block enough times to know that the far more troubling emotions are ambivalence and indifference.

We try to give you something to talk about. To learn about. To react to. The passion you have for pro football often splashes back onto the messengers who point out the possibility that your favorite team may not be the greatest collection of football talent ever assembled.

Regardless, as we close in on 25 years, it only strengthens my commitment to keep it going. Next stop, 50 years. And maybe a lot more than that.

When the anniversary officially arrives next Sunday, I've got a small token of appreciation planned. It's something that the folks who have been in the audience since November 1, 2001 will understand, and hopefully enjoy. (The AWLs of Pardon My Take already know what it is.)

More specifics on that are coming soon. For now, as I think back to those last few days of loose planning and haphazard organization and reluctantly writing a $500 check to the local tech company that continued to honor its quoted price of $50 per month even as the operation consumed more and more space on its servers, it's the perfect time to say thank you to everyone out there who allowed this thing to survive in the lean years and to grow into whatever it now is.

Even if I still don't quite know what it really is.

Either way, hold on to your butts.

item.title: Eagles list Saquon Barkley as questionable; DeVonta Smith, Dontayvion Wicks ruled out
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: The Eagles have left the door open for running back Saquon Barkley to play on Monday night, but they will be down two wideouts against the Cowboys.
item.content:encoded:
The Eagles have left the door open for running back Saquon Barkley to play on Monday night, but they will be down two wideouts against the Cowboys.

Barkley is listed as questionable to play after moving up to full practice participation on Saturday. Barkley has missed the last two games with a hamstring injury and his presence would be welcomed on an offense that's low on wide receivers

DeVonta Smith (hamstring) and Dontayvion Wicks (ankle) were both ruled out on the team's final injury report of Week 7. Makai Lemon, Darius Cooper, Hollywood Brown, Elijah Moore, and Britain Covey are the available wideouts on the 53-man roster.

Defensive back Michael Carter (abdomen) and linebacker Nolan Smith (concussion) have also been ruled out for Philadelphia. Cornerback Jakorian Bennett (knee), tight end Grant Calcaterra (back), guard Landon Dickerson (knee, pectoral), linebacker Jalyx Hunt (knee, ankle), and tight end Eli Stowers (quad) join Barkley with questionable designations.

Bennett, Calcaterra, Dickerson, and Stowers are all on injured reserve, so the Eagles will need to make roster moves to get all or some of them on the roster for Monday night.

item.title: With Troy Aikman possibly exiting broadcasting, he extends an olive branch to Jerry Jones
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Hall of Fame quarterback Troy Aikman has talked openly for years about wanting to work in an NFL front office.
item.content:encoded:
Hall of Fame quarterback Troy Aikman has talked openly for years about wanting to work in an NFL front office. He took a half-step in that direction last year, becoming a consultant to the Dolphins and continuing to work for the team while also working for Monday Night Football.

In March, Aikman spoke openly about the Cowboys’ historical lack of interest in pursuing his services. Now that Aikman's time with ESPN is by all appearances moving toward a conclusion, Aikman seems to be extending an olive branch toward Cowboys owner and G.M. Jerry Jones.

Asked by Mike Fisher whether Aikman would break bread with Jerry Jones, Aikman said this: "I would have lunch, breakfast, or dinner with Jerry any time he wants it. And it wouldn't necessarily have to be because it's a job interview. Just because, you know, we go back a long way. . . . I came in, I was 22 years old. I was his very first draft pick. There's a lot within that relationship, both from the beginning, when he began as the owner, when I began my NFL career as a quarterback for 12 years of my life, playing for him, and then, even in the years that have followed, you know, we've been through a lot. We've been through the highest of highs, we've been through some pretty tough moments as well. Our relationship is complicated. I think he would agree with that, but it is one that's built, I believe, on respect.  This week, he said some really kind things, which meant a lot to me, quite honestly. So, yeah, I would welcome any conversation with Jerry, and quite honestly I don't know if there would be, or if there ever would be an opportunity. But if Jerry came to me and felt that, in his heart, I could lend some services that would help make them better, I would — I’d have a hard time not taking a good look at that."

Jones did indeed speak glowingly about Aikman during this week's quarterly NFL ownership meetings.

"Troy is very capable, and he's so, really relatively speaking, he's in his youth as careers go," Jones said. "And he's very capable of doing any one of a number of things, certainly anything to do with football.  I don't know of any area short of getting that kind of feeling, I don't know of any area that Troy Aikman wouldn't be qualified and competent to go into."

Aikman's current role with the Dolphins remains fluid and undefined, but it was enough to prompt the NFL to place Tom Brady-style restrictions on his ability to enter the facilities of other teams or to attend practices before Monday night games.

Despite Aikman's unfulfilled aspiration to work in a front office, he seems to be realizing that his time as a broadcaster could be ending — and he's apparently feeling some regret over that.

“As I’m into my last year at ESPN, I’m realizing that this is something that could very well be taken away from me,” Aikman told Fisher, via Tyler Lauletta of Awful Announcing. “For the first time, I’m realizing how much I really do — I’ve always enjoyed it. I’ve always known that. But until you risk having something taken away from you, I think sometimes you tend to maybe take things for granted.

“And so, for the first time probably in my career, I’m realizing, you know, this is a great profession. It’s been a great ride for me, and I hope it’s not over. Time will tell. But, yeah. So, we’ll see. I’m excited about what the rest of this year holds, and I’m excited to finally get back into the booth for a Super Bowl.”

With CBS already deciding to make J.J. Watt the full-time replacement for Tony Romo, there may not be a high-profile (and high-paying) seat for Aikman in 2027. If he truly wants to continue to call games, the best spot could be Greg Olsen's current slot as the No. 2 NFL announcer on Fox. And the money that goes with that assignment.

It's still not clear why ESPN has apparently soured on Aikman. Maybe he overplayed his hand, by reportedly asking for $30 million per year. Maybe ESPN wasn't thrilled by his Miami moonlighting, especially since it has complicated his ability to be as prepared to call games as he could be. (It's also possible that Aikman took the position with the Dolphins before running it by anyone at ESPN, which if accurate would tend to impair the relationship between ESPN and Aikman.)

Regardless, Aikman is now making it known that his upcoming free agency sweeps more broadly than broadcasting. He's also officially in play for the Cowboys or any other team that may choose to consider hiring him.

item.content:encoded:
Tank Dell will play his first game in nearly two years on Sunday when the Texans play the Giants.

The team officially activated the wide receiver back to the active roster from reserve/PUP.

Dell dislocated his kneecap and tore multiple knee ligaments in a Dec. 21, 2024, game against the Chiefs. He missed the rest of that season, all of last season and the first six games of this season with the gruesome knee injury.

Dell's rookie season of 2023 ended on a broken leg in Week 13.

The Texans also announced they elevated cornerback Bryce Hall and linebacker Kenneth Murray from the practice squad.

item.title: 49ers activate WR Christian Kirk from IR
item.dc:creator: Charean Williams
item.description: The 49ers made a procedural move on Friday, releasing defensive lineman Ogbo Okoronkwo to make room for wide receiver Christian Kirk.
item.content:encoded:
The 49ers made a procedural move on Friday, releasing defensive lineman Ogbo Okoronkwo to make room for wide receiver Christian Kirk. They made things official Saturday.

The 49ers activated Kirk from injured reserve to the active roster, and they re-signed Okoronkwo to the practice squad. Okoronkwo and linebacker Jalen Graham were elevated from the practice squad for Sunday's game against the Falcons.

The team cut defensive lineman Kevin Givens from the practice squad.

Kirk has spent the season on injured reserve.

He signed a one-year deal with the 49ers in free agency in March and will help Sunday in Mike Evans' absence. The team's top wide receiver was ruled out with Achilles soreness.

Kirk, a second-round pick of the Cardinals in 2018, has 432 receptions for 5,415 yards and 30 touchdowns in eight seasons.

Okoronkwo, 31, has appeared in all six games with one start this season. He has two tackles and a sack.

item.title: Three Panthers players fined for three separate incidents of taunting
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: Only four players across the NFL got fined for taunting in Week 6, and three of those four were on the Panthers.
item.content:encoded:
Only four players across the NFL got fined for taunting in Week 6, and three of those four were on the Panthers.

Carolina's Will Lee was fined $6,377 for taunting. Tommy Tremble was fined $11,941 for taunting. And Zakee Wheatley was fined $5,626 for taunting.

The three were fined for three separate incidents at three different points in the game. Tremble was the only one who was flagged.

It's odd that the Panthers would get caught taunting three times as much as the rest of the league combined, but that's what the league has announced.

The one other taunting fine in the league this week went to Green Bay's Matthew Golden.

item.title: Ravens downgrade QB Lamar Jackson to out for Sunday
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Jackson will miss third straight game with high-ankle sprain.
item.content:encoded:
The Ravens will turn to quarterback Tyler Huntley once again.

On Saturday, quarterback Lamar Jackson was downgraded to out with a lingering ankle issue. It will be the third game missed due to the ankle sprain.

The Ravens could have let the uncertainty ride until Sunday, since they're playing at home. Players listed as questionable often aren't downgraded on a Saturday unless they play for the road team and don't travel with the team.

On Friday, Jackson expressed optimism that he'd be able to face the Bengals.

"Right now, I'm heading in the right direction," Jackson said. He added that pain, not swelling, was the biggest lingering problem.

Jackson said it doesn't hurt when he walks, but that the pain increases when he runs. He explained that trying to play through the pain would only hurt the team's effort to win.

Jackson confirmed that he has a high-ankle sprain, contrary to some of the reporting that described it as something other than that. Typically, a high-ankle sprain requires more time to heal, and it does indeed create more intense and more persistent pain.

He also said that he could know on Saturday whether he'll be able to play, and that he otherwise has a "grace period" until Sunday. The Ravens decided based on what they know as of Saturday to not wait another day before making it official that Jackson won't play.

The team is 3-1 with Jackson starting, and 1-1 without him. Now at 4-2, they face the 3-2 Bengals on Sunday with Huntley getting his third straight start.

The Ravens face the Bills in Buffalo next Sunday, followed by a Thursday night home game against the Jaguars.

item.title: The Dallas Cowboys cheerleaders have unionized
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: One of the NFL's teams has another union to deal with — and the team in question didn't fight it.
item.content:encoded:
One of the NFL's teams has another union to deal with — and the team in question didn't fight it.

Via the Associated Press, the Dallas Cowboys have agreed to recognize the Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders Association as the collective bargaining representative for the team's cheerleading squad.

"The Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders are an esteemed part of the Cowboys organization, deeply respected for the talent and dedication they exhibit," the union said in a statement. "They remain one of the most sought-after opportunities for talented dancers worldwide."

Employers typically prefer to avoid unions, for obvious reasons. Through collective bargaining and the ability to strike, unions can secure better pay and better working conditions for all employees in the bargaining unit.

The Buffalo Jills were the first NFL cheerleading squad to unionize, back in 1995. The Jills disbanded in 2014 after the filing of a lawsuit alleging violations of the New York minimum-wage laws.

Questions about fair pay for NFL cheerleaders have been common over the years, along with allegations of improper conduct. The Washington franchise, while under the management of Daniel Snyder, faced civil claims arising from a "secret outtake" video. Those claims were later settled.

In 2022, longtime Cowboys P.R. executive Rich Dalrymple abruptly resigned amid allegations that he secretly recorded the team's cheerleaders while they were changing clothes. Four cheerleaders received $2.4 million to settle their civil claims as a result of that incident.

item.title: Former Raiders RB Pete Banaszak dies at 82
item.dc:creator: Charean Williams
item.description: Former Raiders running back Pete Banaszak has died, the team announced Saturday.
item.content:encoded:
Former Raiders running back Pete Banaszak has died, the team announced Saturday. He was 82.

"The Raiders Family mourns the passing of Pete Banaszak, whose toughness, competitive spirit, and dedication embodied a legendary era of Raiders football and made him a cherished member of the Silver and Black," the team said in a statement. "The deepest condolences of the entire Raider Nation are with Pete's wife Sue, daughters Rebecca and Amy, grandsons Luke, Austin, and Connor, and all of his loved ones."

Banaszak played his entire career with the Raiders.

The team drafted him in the fifth round of the 1966 AFL Draft, and he retired after the 1978 season. He led the NFL with 16 rushing touchdowns in 1975, which remains a single-season franchise record.

He won a Super Bowl XI ring, which was the franchise's first Super Bowl championship.

Banaszak appeared in 173 regular-season games with the Raiders and played a central role in the famous "Holy Roller" play.

Banaszak, a Wisconsin native, was inducted into the National Polish-American Sports Hall of Fame in 1990.

item.title: With Nick Bosa out longer than expected, 49ers may not have enough healthy players for roster spots on Sunday
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Bosa will miss fifth game with calf injury.
item.content:encoded:
49ers defensive end Nick Bosa pulled a calf muscle in practice on the Thursday before Week 3. Even though the team didn't place Bosa on injured reserve, he has now missed four games. He'll miss his fifth on Sunday at Atlanta.

On Friday, coach Kyle Shanahan was asked about remarks from Bosa indicating certainty he'd return for the Week 7 game against the Falcons and optimism he'd be back for Week 6 against the Commanders.

"I just think he was a little too optimistic, especially for Bosa because he's pretty accurate," Shanahan told reporters. "He doesn't say stuff like that unless it's accurate. I just think it surprised him. He worked out, after he said that to you guys, and the next day he was just a little sore, which surprised all of us. That wasn't a great sign, especially going to play on turf and stuff this week, so I think it was more he was just a little too optimistic.”

Bosa is just one of a long list of injured 49ers players. Shanahan acknowledged on Friday that the 49ers may not have 48 players healthy enough to dress for the game. Has that ever happened to him before?

“No, I don't think so," Shanahan said. "I don't think here. I don't think ever in my career, so it's a unique situation.”

The 2026 season has entailed plenty of unique situations for the 49ers. Through it all, they keep winning. Which makes it Shanahan's best year of coaching (so far), and which has him as the current favorite to be named the NFL's coach of the year.
